events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Sam proposes Sam, Priya. As a Loyal Servant, I know my own allegiance is Good, so I include myself. Priya is an early neutral choice to fill the second slot with no private information suggesting otherwise.

Sam, thanks for the proposal, and I know you're stretching to explain an early pick. I want to push gently, not hard, but here is my concern: Priya was selected with no stated information, and Priya has been quiet so far. That combination is exactly what I would expect from someone who does not want to be questioned about their read of the table. If Priya has a genuine reason to be on this mission, she should give it now, openly, before any of us vote. I would rather hear a real justification late than accept a comfortable pick early.

To be transparent about myself: I am not going to claim I have secret information I do not have. What I do have is a general sense that a team of two is very small, and that a two-person team gives the second player enormous leverage — if the second player is the one who secretly wants this mission to fail, then a random Good player has almost no way to detect it. So the choice of the second slot is disproportionately important, and it deserves better reasoning than "an early neutral choice."

My preference, if you want a concrete alternative for the revision, is Sam plus Leo, or Sam plus me. Leo and I have both been visibly active at the table; either gives the team a member whose judgment we can actually hear. If Priya can articulate why she specifically should be on mission one, I will not block it.

Priya, directly: what is your read on the rest of us, and why should you be on this team over Leo?

Noah, thanks for the direct question. My read so far: Sam has been open about the choice, and I have no secret information to share. I can't claim special insight into the table, so I'll judge by what people have said. Your concern about the second slot is reasonable on a two-person team, but treating my silence as suspicious is a weak basis for that concern. I have been listening carefully and have not yet seen a reason to doubt anyone in particular. I'm willing to be on this team, and I'm equally fine with Sam and Leo if the group prefers that. My main concern is that we don't leave a Good-leaning proposal unsettled over a single unanswered question. Noah, you've said Leo has been visibly active. What specific point from Leo's play makes him a stronger choice than me?

Priya, you asked me a direct question, so let me answer it plainly and then ask you one in return.

You asked what specific point from Leo's play makes him a stronger choice than you. Honest answer: I did not have a quotation from Leo in hand, and I should own that rather than dress up a vague impression as evidence. That is fair criticism of my earlier message. But the load-bearing part of my concern was never about Leo's eloquence. It was about the shape of the decision: on a two-person team, the second slot carries most of the risk, and the only thing we can evaluate about that slot is what the person themselves says. So the question is not "who is more charismatic," it is "does this person give the table a reason."

Your answer, Priya, was that you have no secret information, you have listened carefully, you have seen no reason to doubt anyone, and you are fine with Sam and Leo if we prefer. That is a genuinely good-faith answer to my concern, and I mean that. It also, notably, does not contain a single specific observation about any other player at this table — no claim of the form "X said Y and I read it as Z." It is a statement about your own lack of information and your willingness to defer. Those are two different things, and only the first is a reason for anything.

So here is my question, asked directly: can you give one concrete thing you have heard from another player at this table — Sam, Arjun, Leo, or me — that you read as a Good signal, and can you explain why? And separately, is there anything in your private information, or in what you have noticed in discussion, that makes you more confident about the second slot than I am? If the answer to the second part is no, then Sam and I, or Sam and Leo, is the safer team, and you have told me you are fine with that.

Sam, I want to be clear about my own position so nobody has to guess: I will vote to approve a revised team of Sam and Leo if you offer it, and I am not going to obstruct a team that I think is right. I am only trying to make sure the second slot is chosen for a stated reason.

Priya, I am yielding to you so you can answer those two points directly.

Noah, here are direct answers to your two questions. First, a signal I read as Good: Sam said plainly that he included himself as a Loyal Servant and gave a reason for choosing me, and nobody has pointed to a contradiction in that. Second, I have no private information I can share here, so my confidence comes only from what has been said at the table. Your concern about the second slot would be stronger if you pointed to something I said or did that is actually wrong. So far the only issue raised is my silence, and that is not evidence. I am willing to be on this team with Sam, and I would rather we settle it now than swap in a different player because of a comfort pick. Noah, which specific statement of mine do you think is inconsistent?

Priya, your question deserves a straight answer: I cannot name a statement of yours that is inconsistent with Sam's proposal. I want to be precise, because I notice my own framing has drifted and I should own that. The gap I am pointing at is not a contradiction in your words. It is that your answer contained no independent read of this table.

Look at what you actually offered as a Good signal: Sam included himself as a Loyal Servant and gave a reason for choosing you. That is agreement with Sam's proposal, restated. It is not evidence you gathered. You still have not told the table one specific thing another player said or did that you read as Good, and, more importantly, one thing you read as Evil. Everyone here has been sitting in the same discussion. If you were reading the table the way I am, you would have noticed at least one thing that looked like an attempt to steer the second slot. Silence on that is itself a data point.

I am not claiming secret information, and I want to be clear that I am not asking you to fabricate a read to satisfy me. If you genuinely have nothing, then the honest conclusion is that you cannot distinguish Sam plus Priya from Sam plus Leo on the merits, and the risk profile of the two-person team decides it for us. On a two-person team the second slot is essentially the entire mission: one random Good player has no way to detect a hidden Evil teammate, and mission one is where a single Fail card decides everything. Sam's own inclusion of himself is well reasoned and I do not question it. It is the second slot where we are blind.

Sam, my position is unchanged and I want it on the record before the vote: I will vote to approve Sam and Leo, and I will vote against Sam and Priya unless you revise. I say this as a Good player who thinks a two-person team deserves the more scrutinizable second slot, not as a personal attack on Priya.

Leo, directly, and this is my one question: what is your own read of Priya? Specifically, has she given you anything — one concrete thing she said about another player at this table — that you read as Good, and can you name one thing you read as Evil? If you cannot, I would ask you to vote against Sam and Priya as well, because a team we cannot read is a team we cannot trust with mission one. If you can, then say so and I will take that seriously.

Leo, I am yielding to you so you can answer that directly.

Noah, Priya’s pushback against treating her silence as evidence is reasonable, but it is not a strong Good signal by itself. I have not seen a concrete Evil signal from her either. We have very little to go on, and asking her to produce a specific Evil read does not make Sam and Priya riskier than another unverified pair.

I know I am Good, so I would prefer Sam and Leo to the current team from my own perspective. That does not give the rest of the table a reason to trust me over Priya, though. Sam and Priya is an uncertain opening proposal, not one I can identify as bad from the discussion alone.

Council, I’m Sam. I’ve heard Noah’s case and Priya’s answers. Noah has been direct and has conceded he cannot name an inconsistency in Priya’s statements; his concern is that her read lacks independent observations. That is fair, but it is not evidence that Priya is Evil. Priya answered the questions put to her, did not invent a read, and said she is fine with Sam and Leo if the table prefers. Leo also said he sees no concrete Evil signal from Priya and that Sam and Priya is uncertain rather than bad. I know my own allegiance is Good, so the second slot is the only open question. I have to choose between an unverified Priya and an unverified Leo; the discussion has not given me a concrete reason to treat Priya as the riskier choice. I am therefore keeping Sam and Priya. If anyone has a specific statement from Priya that reads Evil, say it before the vote; otherwise I ask the table to judge this team on the actual record rather than on discomfort with a quiet answer.

I've been listening to this back and forth, and I want to weigh in before the vote. Noah, I understand your point about the second slot being critical on a two-person team, but I think you're applying an unfair standard to Priya. You asked her for a specific read of every other player at this table in the first mission when nobody has done anything yet worth reading. We are on mission one — there is almost no public behavior to evaluate. Expecting Priya to produce Evil reads this early sets a bar that, frankly, no one here could pass without inventing something.

What I find more notable is how hard you've been pushing for a specific alternative: Sam and Leo, or Sam and you. You said Leo has been "visibly active," but as you yourself admitted to Priya, you didn't have a concrete quote from Leo to back that up. So the case against Priya is that she hasn't given enough reads, and the case for Leo is an impression you've already conceded you can't substantiate. That's not a reason — that's a preference.

Sam has kept the team as Sam and Priya, and I think that's the right call. We have no evidence Priya is Evil, Leo offered nothing specific to displace her, and Noah's push for a revision amounts to discomfort with a quiet player rather than any actual signal. I'm going to approve this team.

I want to follow up on my earlier point because the discussion has continued and my position has not changed. Sam has made his final decision to keep Sam and Priya, and I think that is correct based on the full record.

Let me address where Noah's argument has landed. Over the course of this discussion, Noah has asked Priya for specific reads, acknowledged he cannot name an inconsistency in her statements, admitted he had no concrete evidence for preferring Leo, and has now essentially conceded that his case rests on a structural argument about the second slot rather than any actual suspicion of Priya. That is an honest position, and I respect it, but it does not give us a reason to reject this team.

Leo, to your point: you said you have not seen a concrete Evil signal from Priya either. If neither you nor Noah can point to anything that reads Evil about Priya, then the argument for swapping her out is purely a preference for a more talkative player, not a judgment about alignment. On mission one, with no mission results and no behavioral evidence to work with, swapping out a quiet but unremarkable player for a louder one does not reduce our risk — it just changes which unverified player sits in the second slot.

I would rather approve this team than spend a rejection on a coin flip. The proposal is reasonable, Sam has explained his reasoning, and Priya has answered every question put to her. I am voting to approve Sam and Priya.

Priya here. Noah has now conceded three things: he cannot name a statement of mine that is inconsistent, he had no concrete quote behind his preference for Leo, and his case rests on the general risk of a two-person team rather than on anything observed at this table. Those are reasons for caution in general, but they are not evidence against this specific team. Every player has the same mission-one information, and nobody has produced a result that separates us yet. Swapping me out for Leo does not remove the uncertainty Noah describes; it only moves that uncertainty to a different name. If the table is worried about the second slot, the right response is to vote on this team and let the mission reveal something, not to reject a proposal over discomfort with a quiet answer. I am willing to be on this mission, and I will not claim special knowledge I do not have. Leo, you said Sam and Priya is an uncertain proposal rather than a bad one. Given that, do you see any concrete reason the team should be revised instead of voted on now?

Priya, no: I don't see a concrete reason to revise the team based on what we've heard. I would prefer to be on it because I know my own allegiance, but that is not evidence against you or a reason the rest of the table should trust me over you. I will approve Sam and Priya, while recognizing that neither their discussion nor a successful mission would prove both are Good.

Sam confirms Sam, Priya. The discussion produced no concrete evidence that Priya is Evil or that swapping the second slot would reduce risk. I know my own allegiance is Good, and Priya answered every question without inventing information, so I am keeping the proposed team.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Leo proposes Leo, Sam, Priya. I know I am Good. Sam and Priya completed the first mission successfully, though that does not prove either is Good; keeping them offers the best starting point available.

Council, I am Noah. I know my own allegiance is Good, so I want to be plain about where I stand: I have a problem with the second and third slots of this proposal, and my difficulty is entirely with Priya. Leo, you chose Sam and Priya off the back of a successful mission one, and that was a reasonable starting point. But a successful mission is not information about anyone. Evil players routinely let an early mission pass, and a loyal servant has no way to distinguish the two cases from the outside. So "they succeeded together" is not a reason to trust a pair, it is simply the absence of a result. Here is what my problem actually is, and I want to state it as a pattern rather than a complaint. Across two full discussions, Priya has not offered one independent observation of any player at this table. Her mission-one answer was that Sam's reasoning was sound and no one had contradicted her — that is agreement with the proposal, restated. Her second answer was that she had no private information and no reason to doubt anyone. Both are true, and together they mean she has told this table nothing she gathered. A player who has read the table and found nothing alarming should still be able to name the one thing that looked most suspicious to them. Priya has never named a suspicious thing. She has also, notably, never named a reassuring thing about anyone except Sam, and only when Sam was the proposer and the speaker being questioned. That is the gap I am asking about, and it is not a small one on a five-player game where a three-person team almost certainly contains one hidden enemy. Sam and Leo, you are both on this team with her. If Priya had said something to either of you that made sense of who is Evil, say it now and I will withdraw the objection immediately. Priya, directly, and this is my one question: since mission one, have you formed any read at all on who among us is more likely to be Evil than the rest? Name one player, tell me what specifically they said or did that you read as Evil, and tell me why that reading would not apply equally to the others. If you cannot do that, then I am asking you to accept that your place on this team rests on the table's inability to check you rather than on anything you have offered, and I would ask Leo to consider Sam, Leo, and me instead, because I can at least be interrogated on my own reads. I want to be clear this is not a demand that you produce an accusation you do not believe. If you genuinely have nothing, say so, and I will still note that nothing was produced. But please answer the question rather than deferring it again. Priya, I am yielding to you so you can answer

Council, Noah again. My position has not moved: I know my own allegiance is Good, and I will vote against Leo, Sam, Priya and for Leo, Sam, Noah. But I do not want to merely repeat myself, so let me add two new points.

First, the thing I think the table has been circling without naming: this team keeps the same pair because Priya and Sam succeeded together on mission one. A successful mission is not evidence about anyone — it is the absence of evidence. Leo's proposal rests on the logic that a pair who succeeded is a pair worth repeating, and that logic is exactly what keeps this table blind. Evil players gain nothing from good players learning; they gain everything from good players keeping faith in an untested pair. Sam's only mission result is a shared success with Priya; Leo and I have no result of our own at all. The two of us who have not yet been on a mission are the only people here who can still produce fresh information.

Second, look at the record of the last two discussions rather than at what anyone claims to believe. On mission one, Arjun made the longest and most emphatic argument for keeping an unverified player in the team, and Arjun has never once named a specific thing any player at this table said that he reads as Good or as Evil. His contributions have been procedural: the standard is unfair, approve the team. Priya's record is the mirror image of that: asked directly, she says she has no private information and no read of anyone. Neither of them has produced one observation the table could check or falsify. Leo and I have. On a three-person team, if the hidden enemy happens to be the one member nobody can check, the other two are blind for the whole mission — so the team should be the one where at least two members can give each other something testable, which means me and Leo on it rather than two players who have offered nothing to test.

Priya, directly, and this is my one question to you: among Sam, Leo, Arjun and me, name the one you find most likely to be Evil and give me the specific words or behavior that made you think so. If your honest answer is "I have no read on anyone," say exactly that in plain words and I will accept it as the answer I asked for — but I want it stated, not deferred again.

Leo, directly, and this is my request to you as leader: if Priya cannot produce one observation, will you revise to Leo, Sam, Noah? I would rather sit beside a player who can be interrogated on my own reads than beside two players who have offered nothing to interrogate.

I am yielding to Leo so the leader can answer that directly.

Noah, I’m not persuaded to replace Priya simply because she has not named a suspect. Your preference for yourself is understandable, but your ability to offer reads does not establish that you are Good. Nor does the first mission’s success prove Sam or Priya is Good; an Evil player could have played Success. It is still a useful result, though not conclusive evidence.

For now I’m keeping Leo, Sam, and Priya. Priya, since Noah asked for your current read, have you seen any behavior from any player that makes you more suspicious of them, even if the read is tentative?

Leo, tentatively, yes. The pattern I would watch is Noah's. After a successful mission one, he is pushing to replace a team member on mission two, and his test for everyone is the same: name a suspect or be replaced. That is pressure, not evidence about anyone, including me. On mission one he argued for Sam and Leo while admitting he had no concrete quote from Leo, and now he wants Leo, Sam, and Noah, a team with himself on it. Noah, directly: if this team is approved, what specific behavior from Sam or Leo would you check on mission two, and what would make you change your view of them? I am not naming another player as suspicious because I have no read I can back with evidence yet.

Council, Noah again, and this is my last turn on this proposal, so I will say only what the record supports and then get out of the way. Priya has finally produced a read — her first in two full discussions. It names me. I want the table to notice what that read actually is and is not. It is not a claim that I said or did anything un-Good. It is a claim that my questioning pattern is "pressure, not evidence." So her first-ever read identifies the player who was asking the questions as the player to watch. That is the shape of a deflection, not the shape of a read. And notice the tension inside her own message: she says she is not naming another player as suspicious because she has no read she can back with evidence, while in the same message she names me as the pattern to watch. She cannot have it both ways — either she has a read on me or she does not. Here is the record I actually want weighed. Across two discussions, Priya has produced exactly one observation about any player at this table, and it is a characterization of the questioner. She has never named a Good signal about anybody. Not Sam, not Leo, not Arjun, not me. On mission one her only "Good signal" was that Sam's reasoning was sound and nobody had contradicted it — which is agreement with the proposer, restated, and she offered it only after being asked. On mission two, she produces a read of me, only after three separate demands. Compare that with Arjun. Arjun made the longest and most emphatic argument of mission one for keeping an unverified player on the team, and Arjun has never produced a single checkable observation about any player either. The two players at this table who have never offered a readable statement are the two players who most benefit from a blind spot sitting in the second and third slots of a three-person team. On a five-player game, a three-person team almost certainly contains one hidden enemy. If that enemy is a player the table cannot check, then the other two Good players are blind for the entire mission and learn nothing. I will concede what I have conceded before: I want to be on this team, and part of my motivation is self-interest. That is exactly why I am asking you to look at Priya's pattern rather than at my preference. And I will be precise about what I am not claiming: I am not claiming mission one proves anything, I am not claiming Priya is Evil because she is quiet, and I am not asking anyone to invent suspicion. My claim is narrow and checkable: Priya has offered the table nothing that can be tested, she has now turned that silence into a read aimed at the person doing the interrogating, and Sam and Leo are the two players with the most checkable statements

Council, Arjun here. Noah has now used three turns, and I want to answer the case he actually made rather than the one he opened with.

His structural point — that a three-person team with one hidden enemy blinds the other two — applies identically to the team he is proposing. Swapping Priya for Noah does not reduce that risk; it relocates it to the player who has spent this entire discussion arguing for his own inclusion. Noah concedes he has nothing concrete against Priya. His claim is that her silence is itself the signal. But on mission two, with a single shared success and no other results, silence is exactly what a Good player who has seen nothing looks like, and equally what a hidden player who has seen everything looks like. Requiring every player to name a suspect or be replaced is a standard nobody at this table could honestly meet yet — including Noah, who produced no read of his own until he turned the question on Priya.

I will own the same criticism of myself that Noah aimed at me: I have not named a suspect either. What I have done twice is take a position — approve the reasonable proposal, ask for evidence before rejecting a player. Noah's position has been revise, revise, revise toward himself, and he has now admitted that self-interest is part of it.

Nothing in his last message changes the record: Leo said he is keeping the team, Sam explained his slot, and Priya answered every direct question put to her, including his. I intend to approve Leo, Sam, Priya.

Leo, Noah has now asked you twice to revise, most recently in his final turn: is there anything in that last argument that actually moves you, or is your team final?

Arjun, Noah's final argument has not changed my view. His preference for a team including himself is understandable, but Priya's tentative suspicion of his pressure is not a contradiction, and I do not see a concrete reason to replace her. I am keeping Leo, Sam, and Priya. Mission one's success is useful but not proof that Sam and Priya are both Good; this team remains uncertain.

Council, Priya here. Leo, Sam and I are on this proposal, and our only public result is mission one succeeding with Sam and me on it. Noah says that proves nothing, and that is true, but it is still the only information this table has produced about these three players. Noah's revision would replace two players with a pair he has never been on a mission with, and he is asking the table to swap in himself. He has admitted that self-interest is part of his push. His standard is that everyone must name a suspect now or be replaced. Nobody here has mission two evidence to name one responsibly, and Noah himself could not point to a single inconsistency in my answers on mission one. I have answered every question put to me. I have no private information I can share, and I have not seen anything that justifies removing Leo or Sam. Noah's read of me as pressure is an opinion about my questions, not evidence about my alignment. I will vote to approve Leo, Sam and Priya, and mission two should be judged on its result, which is how we will learn more.

Priya here. I have already answered Noah's questions, so I will keep this short. Noah's latest case asks the table to replace two players with himself, and his standard is that anyone without a named suspect must go. Nobody can meet that standard on mission one evidence, and that includes Noah. Leo's team has the only public result we have: a successful mission with Sam and me on it. Swapping in Noah and a player who has never been on a mission gives us less information, not more. I am not claiming to know who is Evil. I am asking the table to approve Leo, Sam and Priya and judge the team on mission two's result. I will vote to approve.

I know my own allegiance is Good. Priya and I completed mission one with zero fail cards; that does not prove Priya is Good, but it is the only public mission result this table has. Leo’s proposal keeps that pair and adds Leo, who is unverified to me just as Noah is. From my seat, swapping Priya for Noah would not reduce uncertainty in the second or third slot; it would simply move it to another player. Noah has pressed hard for a revision toward himself, and he has conceded he cannot point to a concrete inconsistency from Priya. His argument is structural and self-interested, not evidence that this team is worse. Priya has answered every direct question put to her, and Leo has kept the team he explained. I see no concrete reason to revise Leo, Sam, Priya before the vote. I will approve this team and judge mission two on its actual result rather than on discomfort with an unverified player.

Arjun here, and this is likely my last turn before the vote. I want to close on the record rather than open anything new.

The proposal is Leo, Sam, Priya. Leo has kept his team through two rounds of questioning and given clear reasons each time. Sam has confirmed he approves. Priya has answered every direct question put to her across both discussions. Nobody at this table — including Noah — has produced a single piece of evidence that any member of this team is Evil.

Noah's entire case has been that silence is suspicious and that players who cannot name a suspect should be replaced. I have addressed that standard directly: it is a standard nobody can honestly meet with one shared mission result, and Noah himself could not name an inconsistency in Priya's answers. His proposed alternative places himself on the team, which he has admitted involves self-interest.

The practical reality is this: we have one mission result — a success with Sam and Priya. We have no reason to distrust Leo's leadership, and we have no evidence against anyone on this team. Approving this team costs us nothing that rejection would gain us. If mission two succeeds, we are one mission from winning with a clean record. If it fails, we will have a real signal to work with — something we will never get by rejecting teams over discomfort with a quiet player.

I am voting to approve Leo, Sam, and Priya and I encourage the table to do the same.
Leo confirms Leo, Sam, Priya. I am keeping Leo, Sam, Priya. Mission 1 succeeded, though that does not prove Sam or Priya is Good, and discussion offered no concrete reason to replace either.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Noah proposes Sam, Leo. I propose Sam and Leo. Reasoning from the public record only: Sam and Priya have the one shared result we have (mission one success), and Leo led mission two to success, so Sam and Leo have each sat on a team that produced information, whereas Priya and Arjun have both sat on teams whose other members carried the analysis. On checkability, Sam and Leo have each given specific, falsifiable statements about other players; Priya's only observation across two discussions characterizes the person asking the questions rather than any behavior, and Arjun has never named a suspect or a concrete Good signal about anyone at all. On a two-person mission where one Fail card decides the result, I want both slots filled by players whose reads can be tested rather than players who have consistently deferred to the table's judgment. Sam and Leo are also the pair whose combined record is two consecutive successes, which is weak evidence but is the only evidence the table has.

Arjun here, on Noah's proposal of Sam and Leo. Noah, your reasoning from the public record is clear and I will address it directly rather than defer. Mission one and mission two both succeeded, and Sam and Leo sat on those teams. On a two-person mission where one Fail card decides everything, I would like the table to notice what Noah's proposal actually does: it removes the one player he has spent two full discussions pressing — Priya — and the player he has never named a suspect against, me. He has admitted self-interest is part of his push, and he has conceded he cannot point to a concrete inconsistency in Priya's answers. What he offers instead is a standard he invented: produce a readable statement or be replaced. Two missions in, nobody has produced a read he would accept as sufficient.

That said, I want to be fair about the team itself. Sam and Leo are not a bad pair from where I sit. Both have been specific and falsifiable in discussion, both sat on successful missions, and neither has given me a reason to think either is Evil. My objection to Noah's proposal is not that Sam and Leo are dangerous — it is that Noah's case for them is a case against two players he has never been able to substantiate a claim against, and swapping in himself was the stated goal from the first turn.

Sam, you said you would judge this mission on its result. That is exactly right, and I intend to do the same. I will approve Sam and Leo.

I know my own allegiance is Good, so from my seat the open question on Noah's proposed team is Leo. I have no private information identifying Leo as Evil, and the public record does not give me a concrete reason to reject him. Leo was on mission two, which succeeded with zero fail cards, and throughout both discussions he gave specific, checkable statements rather than inventing reads. That does not prove he is Good, but it is at least a record the table can evaluate. On a two-person mission, one Fail card decides the result, so I understand why the table would want both slots to be checkable. I am on the team, and I know I will play Success. I cannot prove that to anyone else, but I can state it plainly. I do not see evidence that replacing Leo with Priya or Arjun would reduce uncertainty; it would move the uncertainty rather than remove it. I also want to be clear that my approval is not an accusation against Priya or Arjun. Priya answered every direct question put to her, and Arjun has been consistently procedural. I simply have no concrete Evil signal from either of them, just as I have none from Leo. Noah's proposal puts Sam and Leo on mission three, and I see no public-record reason to reject it. I will vote to approve Sam and Leo and judge mission three on its actual result.

Priya here. I will not approve Sam and Leo as proposed, and I want to explain why. Noah's draft calls itself a reading of the public record, but most of that record is Noah's own judgment about who asks checkable questions. He has pressed for a team including himself through every proposal so far, and this one again removes the two players he has challenged most. I am not accusing Sam or Leo of anything. Their play is consistent, and Sam has been clear about his allegiance. My concern is the basis for the choice. On a two-person mission where one Fail card decides the result, I want the second slot justified by evidence, not by a leader's preference for a particular pair. Noah has also said Arjun never named a suspect, which is true, but Noah has not named a concrete Good signal for anyone except himself either. If the table can't identify a reason Leo is more trustworthy than the alternatives, I would rather reject this team and let the leader propose again with a clearer rationale. Noah, you have asked everyone else for one concrete statement. What specific thing has Leo said that makes you trust him above Priya or Arjun?

Priya, you asked me a direct question, so I will answer it with specifics rather than generalities.

What has Leo said that I can put on the table? In mission one, when asked for a read of Priya, Leo declined to accuse anyone and then volunteered the sentence that actually mattered for my decision: his own preference for being on the team "does not give the rest of the table a reason to trust me over Priya." He did not have to say that. It was self-limiting, and it was checkable — I could test it against everything he said before and after, and it held. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
